chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Board, the Auditor and the Pay Packet

lessons.title: Auditors: Qualifications, CARO Remarks and Mid-Term Resignations

body.text: The auditor's report is the only part of the annual report not written by management. Read it before you read anything else.

children.text: The chairman's letter, the MD&A, and the investor presentation are all written by the people you are trying to evaluate. The statutory auditor is paid by the company but reports to you, the shareholders, and signs their name to an opinion on whether the accounts give a true and fair view. Auditors rarely say anything dramatic. That is exactly why, when they do, it matters. This lesson teaches you to read the three things auditors use to raise a hand: the audit opinion, the CARO report, and the act of leaving.

Indian auditors follow the Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI. The opinion sits at the very top of the Independent Auditor's Report, and there are only a handful of possible outcomes. Learn the ladder, because the words are chosen precisely.

body.caption: The audit opinion ladder, from cleanest to most serious

cells: Unmodified (clean)
'give a true and fair view'
The auditor found no material misstatement
Normal. Still read the Key Audit Matters
Unmodified with Emphasis of Matter
'Without modifying our opinion, we draw attention to...'
Accounts are fine, but something disclosed in the notes is important enough to highlight, such as a large pending litigation or regulatory matter
Read the note the auditor points to. It is usually the biggest risk in the accounts
Material uncertainty related to going concern
'a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the Company's ability to continue as a going concern'
The auditor is not sure the company can keep operating and meet its obligations over the next year
Treat as a solvency warning. Check debt maturities and cash
Qualified
'Except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion...'
A specific item is materially misstated, or the auditor could not get enough evidence about it, but the rest of the accounts are fine
Serious. Quantify the qualified item and adjust the numbers yourself
Adverse
'do not give a true and fair view'
Misstatements are material and pervasive across the accounts
The reported numbers cannot be used. Exit or do not invest
Disclaimer of opinion
'We do not express an opinion...'
The auditor could not get enough evidence to form any opinion at all
The most severe signal. You are looking at unaudited numbers in practice

body.text: For listed companies, the auditor's report also includes Key Audit Matters: the areas the auditor judged most significant and spent the most effort on, such as revenue recognition, impairment of goodwill, or loans to related parties. They are not qualifications, but they tell you where an expert thinks the accounts are most likely to go wrong. Read them against the business. A software company whose Key Audit Matter is 'recoverability of loans to group companies' is telling you something.

cards.term: 'Except for the effects of the matter described...'
cards.definition: Qualified opinion. One specific area is materially wrong or unverifiable; the rest is acceptable.
Disclaimer of opinion. The auditor could not gather enough evidence to say anything about the accounts.

cards.term: '...do not give a true and fair view'
cards.definition: Adverse opinion. The accounts are materially and pervasively misstated.

cards.term: 'Without modifying our opinion, we draw attention to...'
cards.definition: Emphasis of Matter. The opinion is clean, but a disclosed item deserves your attention.

cards.term: '...may cast significant doubt on the Company's ability to continue as a going concern'
cards.definition: Material uncertainty related to going concern. The company may not survive the next 12 months without refinancing, asset sales, or support.

cards.term: 'We have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence...'
cards.definition: The auditor was not given, or could not find, the evidence needed. Often the basis for a qualified opinion or disclaimer, and often a governance problem rather than an accounting one.

body.title: Name the Opinion
body.question: An auditor's report reads: 'Except for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the accompanying financial statements give a true and fair view.' The basis section says the auditor could not obtain confirmations for ₹410 crore of advances to certain parties. What type of opinion is this, and how serious is it?
options: Unmodified opinion; not serious because it says 'true and fair view'
Emphasis of Matter; worth noting but no impact on the numbers
Qualified opinion; serious, because ₹410 crore of assets could not be verified
Disclaimer of opinion; the accounts are completely unreliable
body.explanation: 'Except for' is the signature of a qualified opinion. The phrase 'true and fair view' appears, but only for everything other than the qualified item. When the reason is that the auditor could not verify advances to 'certain parties', ask who those parties are and why the company could not provide confirmations. That is often a related party or cash diversion question.

children.text: When the audit opinion is modified, LODR Regulation 33 requires the company to file a Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications with its annual results on BSE and NSE. It sets out each qualification, the auditor's estimate of its impact on key figures, and management's response. Watch for qualifications where management writes 'impact not quantifiable' year after year. Do the adjustment yourself.

Illustration: a company reports net worth of ₹1,200 crore and net profit of ₹150 crore. The auditor qualifies the opinion because ₹300 crore of loans to a promoter group company are overdue with no evidence they will be repaid, and no provision has been made.

stats.label: Net profit: if provided this year
stats.context: ₹150 crore minus ₹300 crore, before any tax effect

body.title: Adjust the Book Value
body.prompt: In the illustration above, the stock trades at 1.5 times reported book value. If you fully provide for the ₹300 crore loan, reported book value falls to ₹900 crore. By what percentage does book value fall? Answer as a whole number.
body.explanation: ₹300 crore ÷ ₹1,200 crore = 25%. At the same market price, the stock now trades at 1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2 times adjusted book value, not 1.5 times. The stock was never as cheap as it looked, because a quarter of its book value depended on a promoter group company repaying a loan.

markDefs.definition: Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020. It requires auditors of most Indian companies to report on a fixed list of specific matters in an annexure to the audit report on the standalone financial statements.

children.text: Attached to the standalone audit report is an annexure most investors skip: the

report. It works like a checklist. The auditor must answer a fixed set of questions, clause by clause, whether or not anything is wrong. That structure makes it one of the easiest places to find a problem, because a clean company's answers are boring and a troubled company's answers are not.

body.caption: The CARO 2020 clauses with the strongest governance signals

cells: 3(ii)
Whether quarterly stock and receivables statements filed with banks, for working capital limits above ₹5 crore, agree with the books
Material differences: the company is telling its lenders one number and its shareholders another
3(iii)
Loans, advances, guarantees, and investments given to other entities, including loans repayable on demand or without terms, and to promoters and related parties
Large loans to related parties without repayment terms, or overdue amounts
3(vii)
Undisputed statutory dues such as GST, TDS, and PF outstanding for more than six months
Unpaid taxes and employee dues: a cash stress signal
3(viii)
Income surrendered or disclosed in tax assessments that was not recorded in the books
Unrecorded income found by tax authorities
3(ix)
Loan defaults, wilful defaulter status, term loans diverted from their stated purpose, short-term funds used for long-term uses, and borrowing to fund subsidiaries' obligations
Any default, diversion, or short-term money funding long-term assets
3(xi)
Frauds by or on the company, and whistle-blower complaints received
Any reported fraud, especially one involving management
3(xviii)
Whether the previous statutory auditor resigned, and whether the new auditor considered the issues raised by the outgoing auditor
A resignation during the year, or issues raised that the new auditor could not resolve
3(xix)
Whether a material uncertainty exists about the company meeting its liabilities over the next year
Any doubt about meeting obligations as they fall due

body.text: CARO applies to the standalone accounts. If the listed company is a holding company, problems may sit in subsidiaries. Clause 3(xxi) in the consolidated audit report lists any qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of group companies, so check that section too.

body.title: The Banker's Number
body.textWithBlank: Under CARO 2020, the auditor must report whether the quarterly stock and receivables statements a company files with its ___ agree with its books of account.
body.explanation: Clause 3(ii) covers companies with sanctioned working capital limits above ₹5 crore secured by current assets. A mismatch means inventory or receivables were shown differently to lenders than in the audited accounts, which can indicate inflated collateral to borrow more.

children.text: Under Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013, listed companies must rotate auditors. An individual auditor can serve one term of five years, and an audit firm at most two terms of five years each, followed by a five-year cooling-off period. So auditor changes happen regularly, and a scheduled rotation at the end of a term is routine. What matters is the timing and the manner of the change.

body.title: Auditor Change: Routine or Red Flag?

columns.label: Routine
points: Mandatory rotation at the end of a five or ten year tenure
Announced well in advance, approved at the AGM
Replaced by a firm of similar size and standing

columns.label: Red Flag
points: Resignation partway through a term, especially close to results
Resignation letter mentions information not provided or evidence not obtained
Company's stated reason, such as fees or 'pre-occupation', differs from the auditor's
Replaced quickly by a much smaller, lesser-known firm
Previous reports carried qualifications or Emphasis of Matter

children.text: A wave of auditor resignations at listed small and mid caps in 2018 and 2019, several citing lack of information, pushed SEBI to tighten the rules in October 2019. Auditors can no longer simply walk away mid-quarter and leave shareholders with nothing.

body.caption: What happens when a listed company's auditor resigns

cells: Resigning within 45 days of a quarter end
The auditor must first issue the limited review or audit report for that quarter
Resigning more than 45 days after a quarter end
The auditor must issue the report for that quarter and the following quarter; for the last quarter of the year, the audit report for the full year
Concerns before resigning
Any concerns, such as non-cooperation or lack of information, must be reported to the audit committee, which must share its views with the exchanges
Disclosure
The company must disclose the resignation and the detailed reasons given by the auditor to the exchanges, in a prescribed format
Registrar of Companies
The auditor files Form ADT-3 with the Registrar within 30 days, stating reasons and other facts relevant to the resignation

body.label: Another number to track
body.context: Disclosed in the notes to accounts. A sharp drop in audit fees after a change of auditor, or large non-audit fees paid to the same firm, both deserve a question.

body.title: The Resignation Letter
body.scenario: A mid cap company listed on NSE announces that its statutory auditor, a large and well-known firm, has resigned in the second year of its second five-year term. The auditor's letter, filed with the exchange, says it had requested 'sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding balances with certain parties and the business rationale for certain transactions', which was not provided. The company's own press release says the resignation was 'due to differences over audit fees and scope'. Four days later, the board appoints a small local audit firm with no other listed clients. Last year's audit report included an Emphasis of Matter on advances to suppliers.
body.prompt: What do you conclude, and what do you check before deciding whether to hold the stock?
body.modelAnswer: The auditor's own words matter more than the company's explanation. A large firm walking away from a long-standing client, while stating in writing that it could not get evidence about balances with 'certain parties' and the rationale for transactions, is signalling that it could not stand behind the numbers. The company's claim that it was about fees contradicts the letter, which is itself a governance problem. Replacing it within days with a small firm that has no listed clients suggests the company wants a less demanding auditor rather than to resolve the issues. Link it to last year's Emphasis of Matter on supplier advances: the unresolved balances are probably the same ones. Before holding, read the audit committee's comments filed with the exchange, check the related party note and CARO clause 3(iii) for who those 'certain parties' might be, and wait for the next audit report. Until the issues are resolved and a credible auditor signs a clean opinion, treat the reported numbers as unverified.

body.title: Read the Auditor Before the Chairman
steps: Open the latest annual report from screener.in's Documents section and go straight to the Independent Auditor's Report on the standalone and consolidated statements
Identify the opinion type from the wording, and read any Basis for Qualified Opinion, Emphasis of Matter, or going concern section in full
Read the Key Audit Matters and ask whether they fit the business or point to related parties, loans, or impairments
Open the CARO annexure and read clauses 3(ii), 3(iii), 3(vii), 3(ix), 3(xi), and 3(xviii); in the consolidated report, check clause 3(xxi)
If the opinion is modified, find the Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications on BSE or NSE and adjust net worth and profit yourself
Check the notes for payments to auditors, and search exchange announcements for any auditor resignation in the last five years and the reasons given
Compare with the previous two years: is any qualification or Emphasis of Matter repeating?

points: The auditor's report is the only independent voice in the annual report, so read it first
The opinion ladder runs from unmodified, through Emphasis of Matter and going concern uncertainty, to qualified, adverse, and disclaimer; 'except for' means qualified
When the opinion is modified, use the Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications to adjust net worth and profit yourself; a ₹300 crore unprovided related party loan can erase a quarter of book value
CARO 2020 clauses on bank stock statements, related party loans, statutory dues, loan defaults, frauds, and auditor resignations are high-signal checks
Scheduled rotation is routine; a mid-term resignation citing lack of information, followed by a quick switch to a much smaller firm, is one of the most serious red flags
Since October 2019, resigning auditors must complete the relevant quarterly reports and their reasons are disclosed to the exchanges
